Patañjali’s Yoga Sutras.

## Thence comes speed of mind, the state of bodilessness, and mastery over the primal cause. ॥ 48 ॥

Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable motion for the body. The state of bodilessness is the attainment of the functions of the sense organs—independent of the body—in relation to desired locations, times, and objects. Mastery over the primal cause is the control over all modifications of nature. These three accomplishments are called "honey-like" <note>This term, <term>madhupratīkā</term>, refers to a stage of yogic attainment where the fruits of practice become sweet or pleasant.</note>. These are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the senses. ॥ 48 ॥

## For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the intelligence and the pure self, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience. ॥ 49 ॥

For one whose intelligence has been cleansed of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> <gloss>activity/passion</gloss> and <term>tamas</term> <gloss>inertia/darkness</gloss>, who is established in supreme clarity, who remains in the state of total self-mastery, and who is fixed solely in the discriminative discernment between the intelligence <note>The <term>buddhi-sattva</term>, the purest form of cognitive faculty.</note> and the pure self <note>The <term>puruṣa</term> or conscious witness.</note>, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence. The <term>guṇas</term> <gloss>constituents of nature</gloss>, which comprise all, are determinative...

---

Regarding the accomplishments <note>attained</note> through the mastery of the five forms of the senses, he says: **"Thence comes speed of mind, the state of bodilessness, and mastery over the primal cause."** The state of bodilessness is the instrument-like functioning of the senses that are <note>otherwise</note> independent of the body. Location is <note>places like</note> Kashmir and so on. Time is the past and so on. Object is the subtle <note>elements</note> and so on. Through the mastery of the senses in their connection <note>to these objects</note>, there arises control over all modifications of nature; this is mastery over the primal cause. These accomplishments are called "honey-like" by those learned in the science of Yoga.

One might ask: "If there is mastery over the senses, the senses with their objects may be under control, but what follows for their causes, like the primal cause?" He replies: **"These are..."** This refers to the mastery of the five forms of the instruments, that is, the senses, such as the act of grasping. The meaning is this: these accomplishments are not merely from the mastery of the sense organs alone, but from the mastery of <note>their</note> five forms, which include their causes, beginning with the primal cause. ॥ 48 ॥

He now indicates the secondary manifestations of that discriminative discernment between the intelligence and the pure self—the object for which those forms of <term>saṃyama</term> <gloss>concentrated meditation</gloss>, which are the causes of knowledge, action, and lordship, are performed, either directly or indirectly through the faith produced by the realization of one's own accomplishments: **"For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the intelligence and the pure self, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience."** Through the removal of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>, clarity arises. From that, <note>there arises</note> the supreme state of self-mastery. The mind, <note>which is</note> intelligence, was previously overwhelmed by <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term> and was therefore not under control. Upon the pacification of those <note>impurities</note>, it becomes subject to the control of the yogi who has attained mastery. In that state of mastery, for the yogi who is fixed solely in the discernment between the intelligence and the pure self, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence. He explains this: **"The constituents of nature, which comprise all..."**

---

</margin>

<vocab>Manojavitva (speed of mind), Vikaraṇabhāva (state of bodilessness), Pradhānajaya (mastery over the primal cause), Sattvapuruṣānyatākhyāti (discriminative discernment between intelligence and pure self), Sarvabhāvādhiṣṭhātṛtva (sovereignty over all states of existence), Sarvajñātṛtva (omniscience), Madhupratīkā (honey-like/sweet attainments), Vaiśāradya (clarity/purity of mind).</vocab>

<summary>This page explains the yogic accomplishments—speed of mind, bodilessness, and mastery over nature—attained by mastering the five forms of the senses, followed by the omniscience and sovereignty gained through total discernment between the intelligence and the self.</summary>
<keywords>Yoga Sutras, Patañjali, Vibhuti Pada, sense mastery, discriminative discernment, omniscience, siddhis</keywords>
